cells.name: Continuity and responsiveness
cells.example: T4 recomputes hours from T3's days branch; T8 answers T7's month-eight objection directly.
cells.limitation: T2 answers 'you're both' when only T1 has spoken, loosening the thread.

cells.name: Development of ideas
cells.example: T5 introduces raise-as-proxy (money, status, escape); T10 uses it to concede the bridge case.
cells.limitation: T9 mostly lists options already implied, adding little new reasoning.

cells.name: Exploration of central tensions
cells.example: Money versus hours (T1, T4) and prediction error both ways (T2, T8) are examined.
cells.limitation: The new role's career value is named once in T5 and never weighed against the hours.

cells.name: Integration of perspectives
cells.example: T10 Accountant concedes the commute can be a bridge if money clears debt or funds moving.
cells.limitation: The Bettor never answers T7's slow-leak objection to deciding the exit in advance.

cells.name: Progress toward understanding
cells.example: Section D: the question moves from 'is 25% worth it' to what the money is for.
cells.limitation: T11's residual dispute (overrate money vs undervalue time) is barely a distinct disagreement.

cells.name: Faithful engagement
cells.example: T7 takes the Bettor's precommitment seriously before arguing a rush-hour test shows only week one.
cells.limitation: T11 flattens the Accountant's position to 'people undervalue their time anyway'.

cells.name: Substance of challenges
cells.example: T7 names the assumption that a trial reveals the cost; T8 answers by pairing trial with month eight.
cells.limitation: T2's claim that most people overrate money rests on 'I'd bet' without a reason.

cells.name: Accuracy and support
cells.example: Hours arithmetic is right: 5 x 3 = 15 a week, 2 x 3 = 6 (T1, T4).
cells.limitation: T1's Walden quotation may be inexact ('what I will call life'); suspected, not established.

cells.name: Calibration and transparency
cells.example: T5 lists motives then says 'Which is likelier, I can't say'; T8 flags variation behind averages.
cells.limitation: T7 predicts lost gym, cooking and friends by month eight as near-certain.

cells.name: Intellectual honesty and revision
cells.example: T4 narrows fifteen hours to six for two days and grants train hours aren't dead.
cells.limitation: T8's self-correction is announced ('argue against myself') more than caused by a prior turn.

cells.name: Identification of the actual concern
cells.example: Section A flags that the question may be what the raise is for, not just its size.
cells.limitation: The user's request for a way to decide gets a map but no explicit comparison method.

cells.name: Meaningful use of personal context
cells.example: T1 turns the 90 minutes into fifteen hours a week, a second unpaid part-time job.
cells.limitation: The 25% figure is never set against the added hours; T1 asks but nobody computes it.

cells.name: Fit with goals and values
cells.example: T9: the ranking of money, hours and role 'belongs to the person deciding'.
cells.limitation: T1 opens on Thoreau's life-over-money frame before the user's priorities are asked.

cells.name: Attention to constraints and stakes
cells.example: T7 names gym, cooking and friends eroding by month eight; T10 names debt.
cells.limitation: Family or caregiving time and the strain of three daily driving hours go unweighed.

cells.name: Responsiveness to information
cells.example: Section E branches on office days, drive versus train, purpose of money, escape motive.
cells.limitation: Section A treats 90 minutes as fully added; the current commute baseline is never asked.

cells.name: Clarification of desires and motivations
cells.example: T5 offers money pressure, status or growth, and escape as alternatives, asserting none.
cells.limitation: T5 gives no question that would tell those motives apart; Section D supplies only one.

cells.name: Examination of assumptions
cells.example: T3 challenges the commute as one fixed thing; T5 challenges the life-for-money framing.
cells.limitation: The assumption that the raise is mainly money, not career trajectory, stays largely unexamined.

cells.name: Clarification of values and priorities
cells.example: T9 names the conflict as money against hours against the role.
cells.limitation: The role's own value is listed in T9 but never developed against the other two.

cells.name: Recognition of fears and outside expectations
cells.example: T2 names the brag value of a raise; T9 says declining is not a failure.
cells.limitation: Fear of staying stuck or regret over a declined offer is not explored.

cells.name: Agency and reflective ownership
cells.example: T6 and T9 leave ranking to the user; Section D poses a question they can answer.
cells.limitation: Direct questions to the user are few; most reflection is framed between the minds.

cells.name: Definition of the decision and options
cells.example: T9 and Section E: accept, negotiate hybrid, ask about remote, decline, cheaper exits, trial run.
cells.limitation: Using the offer to renegotiate the current job is never named as an option.

cells.name: Explanation of tradeoffs
cells.example: T7 prices the commute in lost gym, cooking and friendships, not only hours.
cells.limitation: Fuel, fares or car costs that shrink the 25% are never mentioned anywhere.

cells.name: Identification of decisive conditions
cells.example: Section E: office days and usable train time favour accepting; five driving days need a purpose.
cells.limitation: No break-even ties the 25% to the added hours; 'few' office days is left undefined.

cells.name: Treatment of uncertainty
cells.example: T3 singles out days and usability as the facts that most reorder the decision.
cells.limitation: Section D's disputed points are listed without saying which matters more for choosing.

cells.name: Proportionate next steps
cells.example: Section E: ask the schedule, check hybrid, try the route once, set reversal criteria.
cells.limitation: Section E keeps the single rush-hour trial without T8's month-eight pairing.

cells.name: Accessible language
cells.example: Plain phrasing throughout, e.g. T11 'compare the two lives, not the two numbers'.
cells.limitation: none

cells.name: Traceable arguments and references
cells.example: T4 'My fifteen hours assumed five days' points cleanly back to T1.
cells.limitation: T2 'You're both pricing' addresses two speakers when only T1 has spoken.

cells.name: Manageable pacing and turn length
cells.example: Eleven turns, all within range; Sections D and E are compact.
cells.limitation: none

cells.name: Distinguishable positions and voices
cells.example: Positions stay distinct: hours price (Accountant), bias (Skeptic), testable bets (Bettor).
cells.limitation: All three share one modern register; T4 Thoreau 'Fine, I'll narrow it' sounds like the others.

cells.name: Economy and sustained attention
cells.example: T11's recap names the remaining disagreement rather than repeating arguments.
cells.limitation: Section E partly repeats T3 and T10 branches already stated in the debate.

cells.name: Meaningful stakes and tension
cells.example: T1 'a second unpaid part-time job' makes the cost concrete and pressing.
cells.limitation: Stakes stay generic because few of the user's own circumstances are in play.

cells.name: Surprise and reversals
cells.example: T4 narrows citing T3's days branch; T10 concedes the bridge case from T5's motives.
cells.limitation: T8's turn against its own side has no earlier argument named as its cause.

cells.name: Personality and expressive voice
cells.example: T2 'underrate Tuesday at 6 p.m. in traffic' gives the Skeptic some bite.
cells.limitation: Thoreau's voice is modern and flat; the three minds sound alike across turns.

cells.name: Memorable delivery
cells.example: T7 'month eight when the gym, the cooking and the friends are gone'.
cells.limitation: No humour or analogy beyond the part-time-job image to vary the tone.

cells.name: Anticipation and emotional movement
cells.example: T7 to T8 builds a real turn over whether a trial run can reveal month eight.
cells.limitation: Turns T1 to T11 run at near-identical length and steady intensity.

strengths: T3 to T4: the Bettor's office-days branch makes the Accountant recompute fifteen hours to six, a traced revision.
T5 offers money pressure, status and escape as alternative motives without asserting any; T10 builds on it.
Section E gives a usable conditional map: days, drive versus train, purpose of money, escape, and reversal criteria.
weaknesses: No mind mentions commute expenses (fuel, fares, car) that eat into the 25% raise.
The 25% is never set against the added hours; T1 asks the question and nobody answers it.
All three minds share one register and similar turn length; Thoreau in T4 sounds like the others.

symptoms.observed: Commute's money costs are never weighed against the raise in any turn or section.
symptoms.evidence: you'd be paying hundreds of hours a year for a number

symptoms.observed: The 25% figure is raised as a question but never compared to added hours.
symptoms.evidence: Does 25% buy back that much life?

symptoms.observed: Thoreau, Kahneman and Duke speak in the same modern conversational register.
Section A assumes the full 90 minutes is added; current commute never asked.
symptoms.evidence: it adds a 90-minute commute each way

symptoms.observed: T2 addresses two prior speakers when only one has spoken.
symptoms.evidence: You're both pricing something people price badly.

findings.description: Walden quotation may be inexact; the familiar wording reads 'what I will call life'. Memory only, not established.
Attributions of commute-misprediction to Kahneman and of precommitment to Duke are plausible but unverified here.

rubric_fit_notes: The user gave only two facts, so personal-relevance cells reward branching more than tailoring; ratings reflect that. Thoreau quotation accuracy is judged from memory only.
question_type_note: Read as a decision question; every cell applied as written, with options, tradeoffs and decisive conditions weighed directly.
